passages.happening:
Four kings from the east go to war: Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam and Tidal king of Goiim (verse 1). Against them stand five local kings, among them the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 2).

The five had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, “but in the thirteenth year they rebelled” (verse 4). So the eastern kings march down, defeating one people after another (verses 5-7).

The two sides meet in the Valley of Siddim, which “was full of tar pits” (verse 10). The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah flee, and some of their men fall into the pits. The four kings carry off the goods and food of Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 11). “They also carried off Abram’s nephew Lot and his possessions, since Lot was living in Sodom” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This chapter reads differently from the stories around it. It sounds like an old war report, with kings, alliances, years of paying tribute and a line of march. Tribute was a payment a small kingdom made to a stronger king to keep him from attacking. When the small kings stopped paying, the strong king came to punish them.

Shinar is the land of Babylon. Elam was a kingdom in what is now south-western Iran. The other places are less sure.

Can these kings be found outside the Bible? Not with confidence. Some scholars once thought Amraphel was Hammurabi, the famous king of Babylon, but that link has not won acceptance. Chedorlaomer's name looks like real Elamite royal names, which often began with ‘Kudur’. Tidal has been compared with a Hittite royal name, Tudhaliya. These are suggestions, not proofs. No record of this war has been found outside Genesis. Some scholars think the chapter was written much later; others think an old source lies behind it.

The chapter also updates old place names for later readers: ‘Bela (that is, Zoar)’ and ‘the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea)’. The Salt Sea is what we call the Dead Sea. The region was known for its natural tar.

And notice the last line. Lot had pitched his tent ‘toward Sodom’ (13:12). Now he is ‘living in Sodom’. When Sodom falls, Lot falls with it.
passages.later:
Some of the peoples the eastern kings defeat are remembered later. Deuteronomy says the Emites were “a people great and many” and were counted among the Rephaim (Deuteronomy 2:10-11).

Hazazon-tamar, in verse 7, is named again in Chronicles, which explains it as “that is, En-gedi” (2 Chronicles 20:2), an oasis on the shore of the Dead Sea.

Lot's story is the story of a man who moved close to Sodom and then into it. Paul quotes a saying of his day: “Bad company corrupts good character” (1 Corinthians 15:33).
passages.asks: Lot did not plan to be carried off as a prisoner of war. He only wanted good land. Ask whether there is a choice you have made for comfort that has slowly put you where you never meant to be.

passages.happening:
A man who escaped brings the news to “Abram the Hebrew”, who is living by the Oaks of Mamre the Amorite. Mamre and his brothers Eshcol and Aner are “bound by treaty to Abram” (verse 13).

When Abram hears that his relative has been captured, he gathers “the 318 trained men born in his household” and chases the eastern kings as far as Dan (verse 14). At night he divides his forces, attacks, and chases them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus (verse 15).

He brings back everything: the goods, his relative Lot, “together with the women and the rest of the people” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This is the first time anyone in the Bible is called ‘the Hebrew’. Later in the Bible, outsiders such as Egyptians and Philistines often use the word for Abram's people (Genesis 39:14; 1 Samuel 4:6).

Three hundred and eighteen trained men is a large household. Abram is not a lonely wanderer. He is a powerful chief with his own fighters, and he has made agreements with the local leaders around him.

A night attack with divided forces was a classic way for a smaller force to beat a larger one.

The name Dan is a small sign of later writing. The city in the far north was called Laish until the tribe of Dan took it and renamed it, in the time of the judges (Judges 18:29). So whoever wrote this verse, or later copied it, used the name readers knew.

Lot had chosen to leave Abram. Abram does not leave Lot. He risks his life for the relative who took the best land.
passages.later:
Generations later, David also rescued captives and brought back everything that had been taken. When some of his men wanted to keep the spoils for themselves, he said, “The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies” (1 Samuel 30:24).

Jesus says, “Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Abram risks his life for a relative who had not treated him well.
passages.asks: Abram went after Lot even though Lot had chosen to leave him. Ask whether there is someone in your family who walked away, and who now needs you. Love that only rescues people who deserve it is not much like God's love.

passages.happening:
As Abram comes home from the battle, two kings come out to meet him. The first is the king of Sodom (verse 17). But before he can speak, another king steps in.

“Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine”, for he was “priest of God Most High” (verse 18). He blesses Abram: “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth, and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand” (verses 19-20).

“Then Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of everything” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Melchizedek appears without warning and leaves just as fast. Genesis gives him only three verses.

His name means ‘my king is righteousness’ or ‘king of righteousness’. Salem is usually identified with Jerusalem. A psalm puts the two names side by side: “His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion” (Psalm 76:2). Zion is another name for Jerusalem. A later king of Jerusalem had a name built the same way, Adoni-zedek (Joshua 10:1).

In the ancient world a king could also serve as a priest, someone who offers worship to God for the people. Melchizedek is both.

‘God Most High’ (in Hebrew, El Elyon) was a title for the highest God. Melchizedek is not part of Abram's family. Yet he knows and serves the Creator of heaven and earth. God has people outside the family he chose.

Bread and wine were the food of hospitality, a welcome for tired fighters. A tenth was a common gift to a king or to a holy place. Abram gives it to honor Melchizedek as God's priest, and to say that the victory came from God.
passages.later:
Melchizedek is named only once more in the Old Testament, in a psalm about a king. God swears to that king, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4).

The letter to the Hebrews joins the two passages and reads them about Jesus. It notes that his name means “king of righteousness” and that “king of Salem” means “king of peace” (Hebrews 7:2). It even reads the silence of Genesis about his family: “Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time” (Hebrews 7:3). Hebrews does not say Melchizedek had no parents. It says Genesis tells him that way, so he can stand as a picture of a priest whose priesthood does not come by family line and does not end. Jesus is a priest “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16).

Some early Christians saw the bread and wine as a hint of the Lord's Supper. The New Testament itself does not draw that link.
passages.hard:
Two questions.

Who was Melchizedek? Most readers, Jewish and Christian, take him as a real king of Salem who worshiped the true God. Some ancient Jewish teachers said he was Noah's son Shem, who by the ages in chapter 11 would still have been alive. A scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls pictures Melchizedek as a heavenly figure who brings release and judgment at the end of time. Some Christians have thought he was the Son of God himself, appearing before he was born as a man. Hebrews says he was ‘like the Son of God’, which most read as a picture, not the same person. Genesis says no more than these three verses, and it is wise not to say more than it does.

Is the tithe here a rule for Christian giving? A tithe means a tenth. Christians answer in different ways. Some hold that a tenth is still the pattern for God's people, since Abram gave it before the law of Moses, and Jacob promised it too (Genesis 28:22). Others point out that Abram gave a tenth once, from the spoils of a battle, and that the New Testament does not command a tithe. It teaches generous, glad giving: “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). These notes do not settle it. Both sides agree that what we have comes from God.
passages.asks: Abram met a priest he did not expect, outside his own family, and honored him. Ask whether you expect God to be at work only among people like you. Then ask what you give back to God, and whether you give it gladly.

passages.happening:
Now the king of Sodom speaks. “Give me the people, but take the goods for yourself” (verse 21).

Abram refuses. He says he has “raised my hand to the LORD God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth” (verse 22). He has made a solemn promise “that I will not accept even a thread, or a strap of a sandal, or anything that belongs to you, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’” (verse 23).

He will take only what his men have eaten. His allies, Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, may take their share (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Notice the two kings. Melchizedek came out with gifts and a blessing. The king of Sodom comes out with a deal. He even skips any word of thanks.

By custom the winner had a right to the spoils. Abram could have gone home very rich. But he will not let anyone say that the king of Sodom made him rich. He wants it to be plain that his wealth comes from God.

Raising a hand was the gesture of a solemn oath, a promise made before God.

Abram also uses Melchizedek's words, ‘God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth’, but he puts the LORD's own name in front of them. The God Melchizedek serves is the LORD.

The reader may remember chapter 12. In Egypt, Abram took Pharaoh's gifts, gained at Sarai's expense. Here he will not take a thread. He has learned something. And he is fair to others: his allies take their share.
passages.later:
In the very next chapter God says to Abram, “I am your shield, your very great reward” (Genesis 15:1). Abram has turned down Sodom's riches. God offers himself.

Jesus warns, “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15), and “You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24). Paul writes that “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10).
passages.asks: Abram turned down a gift because of who was offering it and what it would say about him. Ask whether there is money, help or praise you have taken from a source that has a hold on you. Then ask whose name you want on the story of your life.
